To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

size is fundamental to understanding shape variation in callitrichid primates, that size-and-shape variables explain a significant amount of the variation in callitridhids, that size is correlated with shape, that size and shape are independent, and that size and shape can be used in combination to discriminate among callitrichids.
size and shape are interrelated and that size is a fundamental component of shape variation in the callitrichine forelimb.

(1) the callitrich forelimb exhibits a significant amount of shape variance that is independent of size; (2) size is an important factor for explaining differences in forelimb shape; and (3) the phylogenetic component of shape variance is strong, despite the presence of significant size differences.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between size and shape in callitrichid primates and the utility of geometric morphometrics in understanding this relationship.
the application of geometric morphometrics to the problem of morphological evolution in the context of size variation and phylogenetic constraint.
size and shape in a phylogenetic context.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
size is important, and shape is important, but the relationship between the two is not always simple or straightforward.
, although size is fundamental, the shape of the callitrihid forelimb is also important and can be used in a phylogenetic context.
the morphometric approach, when applied to a well-defined problem, can be a useful tool for understanding the evolution of shape and the relationship between size and shape in a phylogenetic context.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
size is a fundamental component in understanding the shape of the forelimbs of the three callitrichids examined.
the callitrichids are not a monophyletic group, but that they do have a common ancestry and that size and shape are important variables in understanding the evolution of the forelimbs in this group.
size and shape are not independent and that shape differences among species are more pronounced than differences among individuals of a single species.
The main takeaway from our work is that
size-and-shape and shape analyses should not be considered mutually exclusive.
, in the absence of size information, it is not possible to discriminate among callitrichids using shape alone.
the morphometric technique we employ is capable of detecting and quantifying shape differences in the callitrichids, and that these differences are not “spuriously” related to size.
